description_ru: Вымышленная новость о семивековом споре двух деревень из-за колокола и о хитром решении арбитражного суда.
text:
STRAVENNA. After seven centuries of cordial hostility, a regional tribunal has finally ruled on the ownership of the Great Bell of Santa Orsola, a bronze weighing nearly two tonnes that both the village of Upper Strava and its neighbour, Lower Strava, have claimed since the year 1319. The verdict, handed down on Friday, has satisfied nobody, which several legal observers describe as the hallmark of a successful judgement.

The Arbitration Court of the Northern Valleys, a body whose docket usually consists of boundary hedges and disputed goats, was asked to untangle one of the most ancient quarrels in the region. According to the Upper Stravans, the bell was cast in their own foundry and hung in their own chapel, from which it was stolen by Lower Stravan raiders under cover of a thunderstorm. According to the Lower Stravans, the bell was commissioned jointly by both communities, and Upper Strava simply, and rather greedily, kept it, in the manner of a person who borrows an umbrella.

The evidence submitted over three years included medieval deeds in a Latin so crabbed that two translators resigned, a map on which the river had clearly moved, and a folk ballad of two hundred stanzas, sung in court by a retired baker, which supported the claims of Lower Strava on the grounds that it rhymed.

Presiding Judge Renata Bellweather-Okafor, in a ruling of forty-one pages, concluded that the bell had been jointly owned since its foundation, and that it had been jointly stolen, by each village from the other, on no fewer than eleven separate occasions. "Both parties," she wrote, "have at various times been the thief and the victim. I find this symmetrical and, on balance, rather touching."

The court's remedy is ingenious. The bell will henceforth be hung in a new, specially built tower on the exact boundary between the villages, which the surveyors have identified, after prolonged argument, as the middle of a cabbage field. Each village will be responsible for ringing it on alternate days, and the two parishes must jointly pay for a keeper, who will be selected by lot and forbidden from taking sides. Any attempt to remove the bell by force, under the terms of the ruling, will result in its automatic forfeiture to a neutral third party, which the court has designated as the nearby town of Orvello, a prospect that has horrified both camps.

Reaction in the valley was characteristically restrained. In Upper Strava, a crowd of several hundred gathered in the square to condemn the verdict as "a betrayal worthy of the Lower Stravans." Within the hour, however, the same crowd was observed in the Lower Strava tavern, where it was reported to be arguing, with great animation, about who should pay for the cabbage field.

The farmer who owns the field, a Mr Tomasz Vidal, initially declined to sell, but was said to be reconsidering after receiving what he called "a very persuasive offer, from both sides, on the same morning." He has asked for a statue of himself, in bronze, to stand beside the bell, and for the inscription to be in Latin, to which both communities, for once, have agreed.

The bell will ring for the first time next Sunday. It is expected to sound, according to the bellfounder, exactly as it has for seven centuries: a deep, grave note, rolling down both valleys at once, which each village has always insisted was meant for them alone.

questions.question: How did the judge decide?
questions.answer: The bell was jointly owned and jointly stolen.

questions.question: Where will the new tower stand?
questions.answer: On the boundary, in a cabbage field.

questions.question: What happens if someone removes the bell by force?
questions.answer: It goes to the neutral town of Orvello.
